analysis.one_liner: Creates universal federally funded child care for young children, free for poor families and capped at 7% of income for everyone else.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate committee it was referred to for nearly two years, never receiving a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make every child not yet old enough for school entitled to a child care and early learning spot, regardless of family income, disability, citizenship, or whether a parent works. Families below 200% of the poverty line would pay nothing, and no family would pay more than 7% of its income. The federal government would cover at least 90% of the cost (100% for children of migrant farmworkers and in tribal programs), and providers would have to pay staff wages set through collective bargaining. The bill was referred to the Senate HELP committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children gain most: free care for households under 200% of the poverty line, fees capped at 7% of income for everyone else, and a guarantee of a placement for every child who asks. Child care workers gain from required collective bargaining and compensation standards, and children gain from full-day, full-year services with health, nutrition, and disability supports built in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Every child not yet required to attend school would be entitled to a spot in a child care and early learning program, regardless of family income, disability status, citizenship status, or whether a family member is employed.
Families with incomes below 200% of the poverty line would pay no fee, and no family would pay more than 7% of income no matter how many children are enrolled.
The federal government would pay at least 90% of program costs, and 100% for children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers and for children in tribal and Native Hawaiian programs.
Programs would have to provide services for at least 10 hours a day, year-round, and sponsors must ensure staff are paid compensation set through a collective bargaining process with their unions.

Sponsors would have to guarantee a placement to every family in the service area that requests one, in a setting responsive to the family's needs, with priority for low-income, disabled, dual-language-learner, homeless, and foster children.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation of 'such sums as may be necessary' rather than a fixed budget; the bill specifies no dedicated funding source. States and localities are barred from cutting their existing child care spending to offset the new federal money.

drawbacks.text: The main title is an open-ended entitlement: Congress would be required to appropriate 'such sums as may be necessary' each year, with no cap and no dedicated revenue source, so the cost to taxpayers would grow with enrollment.
Because eligibility is universal regardless of income, higher-income families would also receive subsidies, with their fees capped at 7% of income no matter how much they earn.

Requiring providers to pay union-negotiated compensation and meet national standards could strain smaller and home-based providers, who would depend on the sponsor's federal payments (at least 90% of costs) to cover the difference.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to working families would be large and concrete: care that today often costs $10,000 or more per child a year would be free or capped at 7% of income. The honest cost is fiscal: this is one of the largest open-ended spending commitments a Congress could make, with no financing mechanism attached, and the design spreads subsidies well up the income scale. An honest supporter would concede the price tag was left entirely to future Congresses to fund.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Child Care for Every Community Act on February 9, 2023, with nine Senate Democratic and one independent cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the full action history shows no activity after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No family gained anything from the outcome: the bill died without even a hearing. Federal taxpayers are spared an open-ended entitlement that the bill did not fund, and the existing child care market was left unchanged, while parents of young children and child care workers who would have benefited are where they started.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled an initial group of cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which was referred to his committee in February 2023 and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Senate Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote that would have shown the broader split.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning providers
industries.note: The bill would have routed large federal payments to public and private providers, including for-profit delegate providers, creating a guaranteed paying customer in every community; at the same time it would have required them to pay union-negotiated compensation, meet national standards, and accept capped family fees, which many smaller providers would have found hard to absorb.
The program is universal, so even affluent families would have received subsidized care at fees capped at 7% of income, paid for by general federal revenue rather than by their own taxes alone.
